title: Chief Economists Outlook: counting the cost of the Hormuz crisis, with Maersk's Ilaria Maselli
gist: Maersk's Head of Macro & Markets Insight, Ilaria Maselli, tells the WEF's Radio Davos that the Strait of Hormuz closure has removed roughly 6 million barrels/day of oil supply and could inflict up to ~84% of COVID-19's economic impact if it drags into H2 2026, with 89% of surveyed chief economists now expecting weaker global growth and over 90% expecting higher inflation.

insights.claim: The International Energy Agency estimates the Strait of Hormuz war has created a gap of around 6 million barrels per day between oil demand and supply, roughly 80 days into the conflict, which Maersk's Ilaria Maselli calls one of the biggest crises in the memory of capitalism.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A 6 million bpd deficit is a supply shock on the scale of major historical oil crises, implying sustained upward pressure on crude and product prices as long as it persists.
insights.quote: It is around 6 million barrels per day that are missing, which is probably one of the biggest crises we have witnessed in the memory of capitalism.

insights.claim: Before the war, around 120 vessels crossed the Strait of Hormuz daily; since the conflict began that has fallen to an average of fewer than 10 per day, with many days seeing zero transits.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A near-total collapse in transit volume signals the closure is not partial or symbolic; shipping, insurance and energy markets should price for effectively zero normal flow, not a modest disruption.
insights.quote: prior to the start of the war, around 120 vessels would cross the Strait of Hormuz on a daily basis. And now this is on average a handful every day.
insights.locator: prior to the start of the war

insights.claim: Roughly 25% of global seaborne oil trade and 20% of global LNG exports normally passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the war.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: This quantifies the strait's systemic importance to global energy markets, underscoring why LNG-dependent economies and gas prices, not just crude, are exposed to the closure.
insights.quote: Around 25% of global seaborne oil trade and 20% of LNG exports used to pass through the Strait of Hormuz prior to the war.
insights.locator: Around 25% of global seaborne oil trade

insights.claim: Containerized imports into the Middle East region contracted 40% year-on-year in March 2026 versus March 2025, and containerized exports out of the region contracted roughly 46% year-on-year over the same period, because major Gulf ports like Jebel Ali (Dubai) and Doha (Qatar) became unreachable.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Regional trade volumes are collapsing by nearly half, hitting consumer goods, automotive, chemicals, plastics and aluminum flows; investors exposed to Gulf-facing logistics, retail or manufacturing supply chains should expect continued volume and margin pressure.
insights.quote: in March, imports into the Middle East contracted 40% compared to March of 2025
insights.locator: in March, imports into the Middle East contracted 40%

insights.claim: According to World Bank research cited by Maselli, the oil intensity of the global economy has fallen from about 0.12 tons of oil equivalent per unit of GDP in the 1970s to about 0.05 tons today, meaning the world is far less oil-dependent than during the 1970s oil shocks even though oil remains a critical input.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Structurally lower oil intensity is a mitigating factor that should cap (but not eliminate) the macro damage from the Hormuz shock relative to the 1970s energy crises.
insights.quote: back in the 70s one unit of GDP. It relied on 0.12 tons of oil equivalent, and this number has now been reduced to 0.05.
insights.locator: back in the 70s one unit of GDP

insights.claim: Beyond oil and gas, the Hormuz closure is also cutting off exports of fertilizer and helium from the Gulf region, and helium is a key input for AI hardware supply chains.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A non-obvious transmission channel: semiconductor and AI-hardware manufacturers reliant on helium (e.g., for cooling and chip fabrication) face a geopolitical supply risk few are pricing in.
insights.quote: we have heard a lot in the last days about fertilizers and helium of course that is a key for the AI supply chains.

insights.claim: Iranian authorities are reportedly requesting cooperation and transit-related payments from vessels crossing the strait, but because sanctions apply to Iran and to entities linked to the IRGC, any such payment could expose shipowners, insurers and banks to sanctions risk.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Sanctions exposure creates a legal deterrent that keeps shipping and insurance capacity away from the strait even after a ceasefire, prolonging the supply disruption beyond what a simple truce would suggest.
insights.quote: there are sanctions on Iran and especially on entities linked to the IRGC. So any payment to Iran authorities could expose ship owners, insurers and banks to sanction risk.

insights.claim: US Central Command (CENTCOM) reported on May 19 that it had diverted 89 commercial vessels heading toward Iran and disabled four, indicating an active US blockade operating in parallel to Iranian-side controls.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Vessels face competing blockades from both Iran and the US, meaning even a bilateral ceasefire does not remove all barriers to transit — a structural reason normal shipping volumes won't resume quickly.
insights.quote: CENTCOM, US Central Command reported on May 19 that it had diverted 89 commercial vessels going into Iran and it had disabled four.

insights.claim: Iran has deployed sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz, and a US Defense Department report to Congress estimates that demining the strait could take six months.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A six-month demining timeline sets a hard floor on how quickly normal shipping volumes can resume even after a political resolution, useful for modeling how long the energy supply gap persists.
insights.quote: a report from the U.S. Defense Department to the Congress that argues that it can take six months to demine the strait.
insights.locator: US Defense Department to the Congress

insights.claim: Restoring normal flows through the strait also requires marine insurance to become available again at a reasonable price, which has not yet happened.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Insurance market pricing is a leading indicator to watch for when Hormuz shipping normalizes — before official reopening announcements move markets, insurers' willingness to underwrite transits will signal real risk reduction.
insights.quote: there is the issue of insurance which needs to be available and at a reasonable price to restore the flows.

themes.theme: Chief Economists Outlook survey signal and COVID benchmark

insights.claim: In the World Economic Forum's Chief Economists Outlook survey, the share of surveyed chief economists expecting global growth to weaken over the coming year rose from about 53% in January 2026 to 89% in the July 2026 edition.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: An 89% consensus among professional chief economists for weakening growth is an unusually strong signal; investors should treat a global growth downgrade as close to consensus, not tail risk.
insights.quote: 89% of the chief economists now say they see growth weakening over the coming year.

insights.claim: The share of chief economists who think the global economy might actually strengthen over the coming year fell from about one in five (20%) in January 2026 to about 8% in the July 2026 survey.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: The collapse in the optimist camp from 20% to 8% shows the shift in sentiment is broad-based, not just a rise in pessimists — upside growth surprises are now seen as increasingly unlikely.
insights.quote: In January, one in five of these economists said they think the economy might actually strengthen over the coming year, that's fallen to about eight percent at this point.
insights.locator: one in five of these economists

insights.claim: Well over 90% of chief economists surveyed expect increased inflationary pressure over the coming year as a result of the Hormuz supply shock.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Near-unanimous expectation of rising inflation strengthens the case for inflation-hedged positioning (energy, commodities, TIPS-like exposures) and reduces the odds of near-term central bank easing.
insights.quote: more than 90%, well over 90% of the chief economists expect increased inflationary pressure over the coming year as a result of this supply shock
insights.locator: well over 90% of the chief economists

insights.claim: In the Chief Economists Outlook's severity benchmark, where the economic impact of COVID-19 is scored as 100, the 2025 US tariff turmoil was rated at only about 40, i.e. roughly 40% of COVID's economic impact.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Gives investors a calibrated reference point: last year's tariff shock, already a major market event, was judged less than half as damaging as what chief economists now expect from an extended Hormuz closure.
insights.quote: Now the tariff turmoil rated at about 40.

insights.claim: On the same COVID-19-indexed severity scale, chief economists estimated that if the Strait of Hormuz were to reopen in June 2026, the relative economic impact would score roughly 72 to 100, meaning up to the full magnitude of COVID's global economic hit.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Even a relatively prompt reopening is expected to leave damage comparable to, or exceeding, the COVID recession — investors should not assume a quick ceasefire fully de-risks the growth outlook.
insights.quote: if this was to reopen in June, let's say, what would the relative impact be? And they said about 72 to 100.

insights.claim: If the Strait of Hormuz closure extends into the second half of 2026, chief economists estimate the relative economic impact would score 83.5, or nearly 84% of COVID-19's economic impact on the same benchmark scale.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A near-consensus estimate that a prolonged closure would rival COVID-19 in economic severity is a strong signal to position for a genuine growth shock, not a contained regional event, if the war drags on.
insights.quote: they said 83.5, so nearly 84% of the economic impact of COVID.

insights.claim: Energy costs from the Hormuz shock are already visible in euro area inflation and US CPI prints for March and April 2026.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: The inflation pass-through is not a future risk but already showing up in hard data, supporting near-term inflation-sensitive positioning over disinflation trades.
insights.quote: Already, if you follow a bit the euro area Inflation number, or the US CPI, then you can see that there's been a change very fast, already March and April figures, inflation has gone up.
insights.locator: euro area Inflation number, or the US CPI

insights.claim: Maselli frames the energy price spike as functioning like a regressive tax on households, since higher prices reduce disposable income while wages do not adjust immediately (and may not adjust at all).
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Consumer discretionary spending power is being squeezed in real terms; sectors reliant on household disposable income should expect demand headwinds as long as energy prices stay elevated.
insights.quote: This of course first and foremost is is like a big tax. It just makes everyone poorer.

insights.claim: Beyond the direct energy-price effect, sustained high energy costs are expected to feed into core inflation because energy is an input into production and transportation costs across the broader economy.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: The longer energy prices stay high, the more inflation broadens from headline to core, which is harder for central banks to look through and more likely to trigger a sustained tightening bias.
insights.quote: Energy is an input in a lot of processes and so everything all of a sudden becomes more expensive producing goods, transportation
insights.locator: Energy is an input in a lot of processes

insights.claim: Central banks, particularly the European Central Bank where inflation is a primary mandate, are watching how wages adjust to the energy shock and how long it persists as the key signal for whether inflation expectations stay anchored.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Wage growth data becomes a critical near-term indicator for rate-path expectations — faster wage catch-up would raise the odds central banks hold rates higher for longer.
insights.quote: central banks are definitely looking at core inflation especially will look at how wages adjust to that and how long basically this shock will impact inflation.
insights.locator: central banks are definitely looking at core inflation

insights.claim: The pre-war expectation of a stable-to-declining interest rate environment, including possible US rate cuts, is no longer the base case because of the growth-inflation trade-off created by the Hormuz shock.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Rate-cut trades that were consensus before the war need to be reassessed; higher-for-longer rate risk should now be priced into fixed income and rate-sensitive equity positioning.
insights.quote: the expectations we were expecting prior to the war, a stable environment for interest rates and a reduction maybe in the US for example. This is no longer the case.
insights.locator: expectations we were expecting prior to the war

insights.claim: Maselli argues that if no resolution is found by Q2, oil and derivatives reserves will shrink to uncomfortable levels, causing oil and gas prices to rise again and shortages to spread further.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Reserve drawdowns give a concrete timing mechanism for when the next leg of the price shock could hit if diplomacy stalls — a trigger point to watch rather than a vague ongoing risk.
insights.quote: if no solution is found in Q2, then of course the reserves of oil and derivatives will start to shrink to uncomfortable levels and at that point oil and gas prices will increase again and the shortages will spread.
insights.locator: if no solution is found in Q2

insights.claim: Drawing an analogy to COVID-19's unanticipated second- and third-order effects (supply-chain congestion, a consumption boom, and persistent inflation), Maselli argues economies systematically underestimate the resilience and creativity of households, companies and governments when large shocks hit.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A contrarian counterweight to purely bearish forecasts: adaptive responses (substitution, new routes, new suppliers) could offset some of the modeled damage faster than economists currently expect.
insights.quote: economies tend to underestimate the resilience of mankind and the creativity of mankind when problems like, when shocks of this size emerge.

insights.claim: Maselli flags specific second-order risks to watch, including balance-of-payments strain in emerging Asian countries, possible liquidity crises, transportation-system turbulence, and stress on energy-intensive chemical production in some parts of the world.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A watchlist of second-order transmission channels — EM balance-of-payments and chemicals-sector stress in particular — for investors tracking where the Hormuz shock could surface next outside the Middle East.
insights.quote: some sort of balance of payment problems in emerging countries. I mean, we've seen there is a lot of concern in emerging Asian countries around this.
insights.locator: balance of payment problems in emerging countries

insights.claim: Consumer and business confidence both declined sharply as an immediate first reaction to the war's start, and Maselli argues that a stable, credible ceasefire with a clear timeline for reopening — not necessarily actual reopening itself — would be the trigger that restores confidence and shifts economic dynamics.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Markets and sentiment indicators could reprice on a credible diplomatic timeline well before actual shipping volumes normalize — a potential catalyst to watch that is decoupled from physical supply data.
insights.quote: We've seen as a very first reaction since the start of the war, consumer confidence declining, business confidence declining.
insights.locator: very first reaction since the start of the war

themes.theme: Rerouting precedents and the global choke-point map

insights.claim: Since early 2024, most container vessels have avoided the Bab-el-Mandeb strait and Red Sea due to Houthi attacks on commercial shipping, instead circumnavigating Africa on Asia-to-Europe routes; despite this, no empty shelves resulted because the industry fully adjusted.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A real-world precedent showing global trade can absorb a major rerouting shock (adding ~20 days per round trip) without consumer-visible shortages, when an alternate physical route exists — a benchmark for how much resilience to expect elsewhere.
insights.quote: nobody has seen empty shelves, the industry has fully adjusted and accommodated this necessity.

insights.claim: Unlike Bab-el-Mandeb, the Strait of Hormuz has no physical alternative route, meaning that despite modern technology and logistics resources, global trade remains bound by geography.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Cuts against the assumption that modern supply chains can route around any disruption — Hormuz is a genuine hard constraint, meaning the oil/gas supply gap cannot be resolved through rerouting alone.
insights.quote: in the Strait of Hormuz, there is no alternative. So even though we have a lot of technology and resources in our modern economy, trade is still not fully decoupled from geography.

insights.claim: Trucking goods overland via alternative ports ('land bridges') cannot replace normal port throughput at scale: a single large vessel can carry around 20,000 containers, and each container requires its own truck to move overland.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Quantifies why alternative Gulf ports (Jeddah, Salalah, Khor Fakkan) are only a partial workaround, not a substitute for Hormuz-dependent ports — regional logistics bottlenecks should persist.
insights.quote: when a big vessel arrives in a port it can have 20,000 containers and each container goes on one truck. So you need a lot of trucks to replace the agility of normal port operations

insights.claim: The US is expected to export more oil this year than previously expected, but the increase amounts to only hundreds of thousands of additional barrels — far too small to offset the roughly 6 million barrel-per-day gap created by the Hormuz closure.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: US shale supply growth is not a credible near-term offset to the Hormuz shortfall, undercutting narratives that US production alone can neutralize the price impact.
insights.quote: the US will export more this year than expected, but we're talking about hundreds of thousands of barrels, not huge amounts that can by far not compensate for this.

insights.claim: Building additional oil pipelines as a longer-term alternative to Hormuz is being discussed, but such infrastructure takes years to build, is expensive, and is especially difficult to construct during an active conflict.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Structural fixes to Hormuz dependency are a multi-year story, not a near-term solution — investors should not expect pipeline capacity to materially change the supply picture in 2026 or 2027.
insights.quote: something that is being discussed at this moment is also building more pipelines. But that is something else, of course, that doesn't happen within weeks. And it's especially difficult to do in the time of a conflict.

insights.claim: The Panama Canal is flagged as a second major global choke point at risk, due to scientists' warnings about El Nino-driven low water levels this year (a repeat of a 2023 episode that reduced ship transits); it is individually less disruptive than Hormuz because ships can reroute around it, but Maselli warns that closures of multiple straits at once compound into a serious capacity constraint.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Investors should monitor Panama Canal water levels as a second, independent choke-point risk; simultaneous stress across Hormuz, Bab-el-Mandeb and Panama would compound shipping capacity constraints beyond what any single closure implies.
insights.quote: If you start closing more than one strait that, you know, when you sum it up, it can become problematic to deal with.

themes.theme: Trade turns from growth engine to geopolitical weapon

insights.claim: Maselli argues the dominant view of trade and supply chains has structurally shifted: for a long time they were mostly treated as a tool for economic growth, but they are now increasingly treated as a tool for foreign policy and security policy.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A framework for interpreting tariffs, export controls and choke-point disputes not as isolated events but as a durable regime change in how governments use trade — relevant for long-horizon positioning in globally exposed sectors.
insights.quote: for a long time, they were mostly a tool for economic growth. And now they are rather a tool for foreign policy and security policy.

insights.claim: Maselli references a quote from Italian intellectual Antonio Gramsci — 'the old world is dying, the new world is struggling to be born, so now is the time for monsters' — to frame the present period as a structural transition phase for the global order in which disruptions are effectively inevitable, not one-off events.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Signals that repeated geopolitical shocks (Hormuz, Red Sea, tariffs, trade-bloc realignment) should be treated as a recurring regime, not isolated tail events, when building risk models for the next several years.
insights.quote: the old world is dying the new world is struggling to be born so now is the time for monsters

insights.claim: The US blanket 10% tariff on all imports, which followed a Supreme Court ruling on the IEEPA legal authority, is set to expire in July 2026, but new tariffs are expected to follow with the specific countries, sectors and rates still undetermined.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A near-term US trade-policy catalyst with unresolved scope — sector- and country-exposed companies face a period of tariff-rate uncertainty through the summer.
insights.quote: in July, the 10% tariffs on all U.S. Imports will expire. The one that followed the IEBA ruling of the Supreme Court.
insights.locator: 10% tariffs on all U.S. Imports will expire

insights.claim: The USMCA renegotiation is looming this summer, with Mexico positioning itself to align closely with US trade policy while Canada has taken a more adversarial, clashing stance toward the US.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Divergent Mexico/Canada positioning ahead of USMCA renegotiation implies asymmetric trade-policy risk for the two economies — Mexico may see relatively smoother terms while Canada faces a more contentious negotiation.
insights.quote: Mexico has done its best to align itself to the trade policy of the US and Canada is in a different position, is more in a clashing position with the US
insights.locator: Mexico has done its best to align

insights.claim: Concern is building in multiple capitals about protectionism against China, driven by Chinese exports having been 'incredibly strong' over the past three years in a way that risks crowding out exports and domestic production in other countries.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Rising anti-China protectionist sentiment across multiple governments increases the probability of further tariff or trade-barrier action against Chinese exporters, a risk for China-exposed manufacturers and a potential tailwind for import-competing domestic producers elsewhere.
insights.quote: we've seen Chinese exports incredibly strong in the last three years, possibly crowding out experts from other places or even domestic production in some countries.

insights.claim: In contrast to rising protectionism elsewhere, previously-stalled trade agreements such as EU-Mercosur and EU-India have both been signed, positioning the EU and India as new centers of trade-policy dynamism.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A counter-trend to watch alongside rising protectionism: EU and India trade liberalization could open new market access and investment opportunities even as US-China and related trade tensions intensify.
insights.quote: trade agreements that were impossible, like EU-Mercosur or EU-India, have all of a sudden been signed.

themes.theme: Three-force framework for the 2026 growth outlook

insights.claim: Maselli frames the net path of the global economy in 2026 as depending on the balance between three forces: the negative drag of the energy/oil shock, the positive pull of an AI investment boom fueling growth in the US and in Asian economies such as Korea and Taiwan, and supportive fiscal policy.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A concise three-factor model for tracking the net 2026 growth trajectory — investors should watch AI capex momentum and fiscal stance as counterweights that could offset some of the energy-shock drag, rather than viewing the Hormuz crisis in isolation.
insights.quote: There is definitely, of course, the energy shock we discussed at length. There is also this AI investment boom that keeps fueling growth in the US and in a lot of countries in Asia, like Korea, like Taiwan, for example.
insights.locator: the energy shock we discussed at length

insights.claim: Large fiscal deficits are providing a cushion for growth: the US fiscal deficit was about 6% of GDP last year, and the euro area's deficit was close to 3% of GDP.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Sizeable fiscal support (especially the 6%-of-GDP US deficit) is a structural offset to the energy shock and inflation drag, relevant to debates about how much fiscal room remains before deficits themselves become a market concern.
insights.quote: In the U.S. Last year, the fiscal deficit was 6% of GDP, we're talking about 6% or huge GDP, so a lot of support for the economy and close to 3% in the euro area also.
